docs.title: Cochleogram
docs.text: Cochleogram is a desktop application for analyzing confocal microscopy images of the cochlea. It supports two distinct workflows depending on how your tissue was imaged.

docs.title: Frequency map — full cochlea scan
docs.text:
Use this workflow when you imaged the entire cochlear length at low magnification, broken into multiple overlapping pieces from base to apex.

You align the image tiles, trace the IHC spiral across all pieces, and export a composite image with tonotopic frequency labels.

→ Frequency Map workflow

docs.title: Cell counting — ROI scan
docs.text:
Use this workflow when you imaged specific frequency regions at high magnification (e.g., 63×) to count hair cells.

You trace a spiral through each row of cells (IHC, OHC1–3), run automated detection, and correct the results manually. The spiral length is used to calculate cells per 100 µm.

→ Cell Counting workflow

docs.text: Format Extra required Leica .lif pip install cochleogram[lif] Zeiss .czi pip install cochleogram[czi] Imaris .ims pip install cochleogram[ims]

docs.title: Supported species

Species Frequency range Mouse ~3–80 kHz Gerbil ~0.1–50 kHz

docs.title: Cell Counting Workflow
docs.text:
Use this workflow when you have imaged specific cochlear regions at high magnification (typically 63×) to count hair cells at defined frequencies.

Goal: count IHC and OHC cells per 100 µm at each imaged frequency location.

The spiral serves two purposes in this workflow: it guides the automated cell-detection algorithm, and it provides the total path length used to calculate cells per 100 µm.

docs.title: File naming
docs.text:
Name each tile with its target frequency using the <n>p<d>_kHz pattern:

G017-1R_8p0_kHz.lif     ← 8.0 kHz
G017-1R_16p0_kHz.lif    ← 16.0 kHz
G017-1R_32p0_kHz.lif    ← 32.0 kHz

Cochleogram reads the frequency from the filename and associates it with that tile.

docs.title: Step 1: Load the data
docs.text:
1. Open the File menu.
  2. Choose ROI scans.
  3. Navigate to your file or folder.

Each tile loads into its own tab, labeled by frequency.

docs.title: Step 2: Trace spirals through each row
docs.text:
Switch to Spiral mode by pressing S.

Unlike the frequency map workflow, you need a separate spiral for every row of cells — IHC and all three OHC rows. The spiral length for each row is used to normalize the cell count.

Work through each row in turn:

Key Row I Inner Hair Cells (IHC) 1 Outer Hair Cells row 1 (OHC1) 2 Outer Hair Cells row 2 (OHC2) 3 Outer Hair Cells row 3 (OHC3)

For each row:

  1. Select the row with the key above.
  2. Right-click to place nodes along that row. You need at least 4 nodes.
  3. The app fits a smooth B-spline through your nodes.

IHC spiral traced at 32 kHz. Square markers = nodes you placed; the curve fits through them automatically.

Repeat for OHC1, OHC2, and OHC3.

docs.title: Step 3: Detect cells
docs.text:
Switch to Cell mode by pressing C.

Automatic detection:

For each row:

  1. Select the row (I, 1, 2, or 3).
  2. Set the search parameters in the toolbar:
  3. Find cells within — how far from the spline to search (µm)
  4. with a spacing of — minimum distance between detected cells (µm)
  5. using — which channel to detect on (typically CtBP2 for IHC, MyosinVIIa for OHC)
  6. Click Count.

Cells detected across all rows. White circles = IHC; colored dots = OHC1–3.

Manual corrections:

Action Result Right-click Add a cell Shift+right-click Remove a cell

Run Count and correct for each row before moving on.

docs.title: Step 4: Mark extra (supernumerary) OHCs
docs.text:
Occasionally a fourth row of outer hair cells appears that does not fall cleanly along OHC1–3. These are supernumerary cells and should be counted separately.

Press 4 to select the Extra row, then right-click to mark each supernumerary cell individually. These cells are tracked independently and do not affect the OHC1–3 counts.

docs.title: Step 5: Save
docs.text: Press Ctrl+S or go to File → Save analysis.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text: Key Action S Spiral mode C Cell mode I Select IHC row 1 / 2 / 3 Select OHC row 1 / 2 / 3 4 Select Extra (supernumerary) row Ctrl+S Save analysis Esc Cancel in-progress action

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Count marks noise or misses cells. Adjust the search width and spacing before running. A tighter width (e.g., 2.5 µm) reduces false positives; a smaller spacing value catches closely-packed cells. Clean up the remainder manually.

I have cells that fall between the standard OHC rows. Use the Extra row (4) for supernumerary OHCs. Do not force them onto OHC1–3.

A row is unusable (e.g., missing tissue, poor histology). Select that row and mark it as Unratable in the toolbar. This excludes that specific row from counts. Each row has its own Unratable flag — marking IHC as unratable does not affect OHC counts, and vice versa.

docs.title: Frequency Map Workflow
docs.text:
Use this workflow when you have imaged the full cochlear length at low magnification. The cochlea is typically captured as a series of overlapping pieces running from the hook (base, high frequency) to the apex (low frequency).

Goal: produce a composite image with tonotopic frequency labels overlaid on the IHC spiral.

docs.title: File naming
docs.text:
Name each piece file with a numbered suffix in order from base to apex:

B009-8L_piece_1.lif   ← hook / base (high frequency)
B009-8L_piece_2.lif
B009-8L_piece_3.lif
...
B009-8L_piece_7.lif   ← apex (low frequency)

Cochleogram uses the piece numbers to assemble the cochlea in the correct order.

Note

If a piece is missing (e.g., lost tissue), it can be substituted from another animal. Add a _copied_<note> suffix to the filename — the composite figure will label it accordingly.

docs.title: Step 1: Load the data
docs.text:
1. Open the File menu.
  2. Choose Full cochlea scan.
  3. Navigate to your file or folder.

Cochleogram detects the format automatically (.lif, .czi, or .ims) and loads each piece into its own tab.

docs.title: Step 2: Align tiles
docs.text:
Note

Skip this step if each piece is a single image with no overlap.

Each piece may contain multiple overlapping tiles that need to be registered before tracing.

Switch to Tile mode by pressing T.

Automatic alignment (recommended):

Click Align tiles. Cochleogram cross-correlates adjacent tiles using the MyosinVIIa channel.

Manual adjustment:

  1. Press N / P to cycle through tiles within a piece.
  2. Use the arrow keys to nudge the selected tile.
  3. Toggle Highlight selected to show a red border around the active tile.

Repeat for each piece before moving on.

docs.title: Step 3: Trace the spiral
docs.text:
Switch to Spiral mode by pressing S.

For a frequency map, you only need to trace one row. IHC is the standard choice, but any row works — the frequency calculation depends on distance along the spiral, not which row you use.

Select the row with I (IHC), then for each piece:

  1. Right-click to place nodes along the hair cell row. You need at least 4 nodes per piece.
  2. Cochleogram fits a smooth B-spline curve through your nodes automatically.
  3. Nodes can be placed in any order — the app determines the correct path.

Setting the basal origin:

The first node placed becomes the origin (basal end). To reassign the origin to a different node, Ctrl+right-click that node.

The origin matters — it anchors the frequency scale. Make sure it sits at the basal (high-frequency) end of the cochlea.

Trace the spiral through every piece from base to apex before generating the map.

docs.title: Step 4: Save your work
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+S or go to File → Save analysis.

Analysis state is saved as JSON files alongside your data:

B009-8L_piece_1_analysis.json
B009-8L_piece_2_analysis.json
...

docs.title: Step 5: Generate the frequency map
docs.text:
Go to File → Generate composite (frequency map) or press Ctrl+F.

Configure the export:

Setting Description Species Mouse or Gerbil — determines the tonotopic frequency equation Frequency range Low and high bounds (kHz) for the labels Octave step How often frequency labels appear along the spiral Channels Which fluorescence channels to include in the composite File format PDF (recommended for publication), TIFF, or JPEG

Click Generate to export.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text: Key Action T Tile mode S Spiral mode I Select IHC row 1 / 2 / 3 Select OHC row 1 / 2 / 3 N / P Next / previous tile Ctrl+S Save analysis Ctrl+F Generate frequency map

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide covers installation and helps you choose the right workflow for your data.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
You need Python 3.7 or later. Install Cochleogram from PyPI using pip. Include the extras that match your file format:

# Leica (.lif) files
pip install cochleogram[lif]

# Zeiss (.czi) files
pip install cochleogram[czi]

# Both formats
pip install cochleogram[lif,czi]

# Imaris (.ims) files
pip install cochleogram[ims]

Verify the installation:

cochleogram --version

docs.title: Launching the app
docs.text:
cochleogram

To open a specific dataset immediately:

cochleogram /path/to/your/data

The app remembers the last dataset you opened.

docs.title: Which workflow do you need?
docs.text: Cochleogram has two distinct modes. Choose based on how your tissue was imaged.

docs.title: Frequency map (full cochlea scan)
docs.text:

Goal: produce a composite image with tonotopic frequency labels.

Steps: align image tiles → trace the IHC spiral across all pieces → export the frequency map.

docs.title: Cell counting (ROI scan)
docs.text:
Use this when you imaged specific frequency regions at high magnification (e.g., 63×) to count hair cells.

Goal: count IHC and OHC cells per 100 µm at defined frequencies.

Steps: trace a spiral through each hair cell row → detect cells → review and correct.
